passage.text: Effect of Aficamten on Cardiac Structure and Function in Patients With Symptomatic Nonobstructive Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy
BACKGROUND:

Aficamten significantly improved both functional capacity and patient-reported health status in patients with symptomatic nonobstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy in the phase 3 randomized, placebo-controlled ACACIA-HCM trial (Assessment Comparing Aficamten to Placebo on Cardiac Endpoints in Adults with Non-Obstructive HCM; NCT06081894). Serial echocardiographic examinations may provide insights into the mechanisms underlying the therapeutic effect of aficamten in this prespecified exploratory analysis.
METHODS:

Symptomatic patients with nonobstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy were randomized 1:1 to receive aficamten (range, 5–20 mg, titration based on left ventricular [LV] ejection fraction) or placebo for up to 72 weeks (end of treatment). The effect of aficamten on echocardiographic measures at 36 weeks (time of primary end point) and end of treatment was assessed with linear regression models adjusted for baseline values, intracavity obstruction, and baseline atrial fibrillation.
RESULTS:

Among 517 participants (mean±SD: age, 55±16 years; 54% female, 75% White, 13% Asian), mean baseline LV ejection fraction was 68±4% with abnormal measures of diastolic function. Compared with placebo, aficamten decreased LV ejection fraction (−4.6% [−5.5, −3.6]; P<0.001) at 36 weeks and increased LV volumes. Aficamten improved measures of diastolic function, including lateral e’ and septal e’ velocities, at 36 weeks (0.9 cm/s [0.6, 1.2] and 0.7 cm/s [0.4, 0.9], respectively; P<0.001 for both) and at end of treatment (0.9 cm/s [0.5, 1.2] and 0.9 cm/s [0.6, 1.1], respectively; P<0.001 for both) and septal E/e’ by end of treatment (−1.4 [−2.1, −0.6]; P<0.001, respectively). Peak tricuspid regurgitation velocity improved at 36 weeks (−10.4 cm/s [−19.9, −1.0]; P=0.030) with a sustained effect through end of treatment. Left atrial volume index did not significantly improve at 36 weeks (−1.3 [95% CI, −2.6, 0.04]; P=0.06) but showed a trend towards improvement with longer treatment exposure (−1.7 [−3.2, −0.3]; P=0.022). Aficamten demonstrated incremental improvements in measures of LV structure and function compared to placebo as doses were increased, with improvement in diastolic indices evident by week 2 of titration.
CONCLUSIONS:

In patients with nonobstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, aficamten improved echocardiographic measures of diastolic function. These findings suggest that the benefits of aficamten extend beyond the effects of LV outflow tract gradient reduction observed in prior studies.
REGISTRATION:
URL: https://www.clinicaltrials.gov; Unique identifier: NCT06081894.
Clinical Perspective
What Is New?

In symptomatic patients with nonobstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, aficamten compared with placebo significantly improved echocardiographic measures of left ventricular (LV) diastolic function over 36 weeks and/or by end of treatment (up to 72 weeks).

Aficamten treatment resulted in a modest reduction in LV systolic function yet remained within normal range, similar to the reductions demonstrated in patients with obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
What Are the Clinical Implications?

The improvement in LV diastolic function with aficamten in nonobstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy was associated with improvement in exercise capacity, patient-reported health status, and NT-proBNP (N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide), supporting the clinical importance of LV diastolic function in nonobstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.

These findings expand the observed cardiovascular effects of aficamten to patients with nonobstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, in whom improvement in LV diastolic function was observed in the absence of LV outflow tract obstruction.
Editorial, see p 1577

Symptom burden in patients with nonobstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (nHCM) has been attributed to diastolic dysfunction, myocardial fibrosis, impaired myocardial energetics, microvascular ischemia, and left atrial myopathy. Providing effective treatment for patients with symptomatic nHCM has been a therapeutic challenge with no proven therapies to address the pathophysiology and substantial morbidity associated with the disease.

Aficamten, a next-in-class cardiac myosin inhibitor that reduces actin-myosin cross-bridges within the cardiomyocyte sarcomere, has demonstrated clinical efficacy in obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (oHCM) with improvement in exercise capacity and patient-reported health status, as well as improvement in measures of left ventricular (LV) diastolic function, LV outflow tract gradients, mitral valve systolic anterior motion, and mitral regurgitation. In the phase 3 randomized, placebo-controlled ACACIA-HCM trial (Assessment Comparing Aficamten to Placebo on Cardiac Endpoints in Adults with Non-obstructive HCM), aficamten also improved exercise capacity and patient-reported health status, as well as heart failure symptoms and NT-proBNP (N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide) in patients with symptomatic nHCM. This study analyzes the serial echocardiographic examinations performed in ACACIA-HCM to characterize the therapeutic effect of aficamten on cardiac structure and function in patients with nHCM.
Methods
Study Design and Procedures

ACACIA-HCM (NCT06081894) was a phase 3, multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in which patients with symptomatic nHCM were randomized 1:1 to aficamten (range, 5–20 mg, titration based on LV ejection fraction [LVEF] over the first 6 weeks) or placebo for up to 72 weeks, with a 4-week washout period. The aficamten dose was increased at weeks 2, 4, and 6 in those with LVEF ≥60%. For LVEF ≥50% to <60%, the dose was maintained; for LVEF <50%, the dose was reduced; and for LVEF <40%, aficamten was temporarily discontinued. A total of 517 patients were enrolled from 160 sites between August 2023 and March 2025. Dual primary end points of change in Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire Clinical Summary Score (KCCQ-CSS) and peak oxygen uptake (pVO2) were assessed at 36 weeks. Secondary end points included New York Heart Association functional class, the composite Z score of pVO2 and ventilatory efficiency, NT-proBNP, left atrial volume index (LAVI) in patients without atrial fibrillation or flutter on baseline ECG, and time to first composite cardiovascular event. Inclusion and exclusion criteria are given in Table S1. The protocol was approved by an institutional review board or independent ethics committee at each site, and patients provided written informed consent prior to enrollment.

Serial echocardiograms were obtained at baseline; weeks 2, 4, 6, 8, 12, 24, 36, 48, 60, and 72;end of treatment (EoT); and end of study, the first 4 of which were used to guide dose titration. Certified sonographers used a prespecified protocol to perform all echocardiograms. Both the sonographers and interpreting cardiologists were blinded to treatment assignment and were not otherwise involved in the study. A core laboratory (Brigham and Women’s Hospital Cardiovascular Imaging Core Laboratory) performed blinded analysis according to the American Society of Echocardiography guidelines using commercially available software (US2.ai). Titration was performed according to site-reported LVEF. Reproducibility metrics of the core laboratory measures have been previously reported. Standard measurements for cardiac structure and function were performed: LV end-diastolic volume index, LV end-systolic volume index, LV end-diastolic diameter, LV end-systolic diameter, LVEF (modified Simpson’s method), septal and lateral early diastolic mitral annular velocity (septal e’ and lateral e’ velocity, respectively), ratio between early mitral inflow velocity and septal and lateral mitral annular early diastolic velocity (septal E/e’ and lateral E/e’ ratio, respectively), LV outflow tract gradients at rest and during Valsalva, LV outflow tract velocity-time integral, LV stroke volume (Doppler method), cardiac output, tricuspid annular plane systolic excursion, right ventricular (RV) s’ velocity, and peak tricuspid regurgitation velocity. LV global longitudinal and circumferential strain were assessed with vendor-independent software (TOMTEC) using speckle tracking of the endocardial and mid-myocardial layer, respectively.
Statistical Analysis

In this post hoc exploratory analysis, statistical analyses were prespecified without specification of all echocardiographic measures. Baseline values and within-group treatment changes from baseline to week 36 and EoT are reported as mean±SD. The primary analysis assessed the between-group treatment difference at week 36. EoT and end of study between-group treatment differences were also assessed among participants with available data (focused examinations with limited measures were performed at the end of study).

Different statistical methods were used to evaluate the treatment effect on LAVI compared with the remainder of the echocardiographic measures. The primary ACACIA-HCM analysis included LAVI as a secondary end point and excluded those with atrial fibrillation on screening ECG. Analysis of the change from baseline to week 36 was performed with ANCOVA with the baseline value, treatment group, and randomization stratification factors (persistent atrial fibrillation and presence of intracavitary obstruction, both as defined by the site investigator) as covariates. Missing data for LAVI for the primary analysis at week 36 were multiply imputed with previously described methods; for the EoT LAVI analysis, missing data were imputed using the most recent value available between week 36 and EoT or, if not available, using week 36 values if available to evaluate for additional treatment effect beyond 36 weeks of treatment.

For the remaining echocardiographic measures in this prespecified analysis, the treatment effect on serial echocardiographic measures at 36 weeks was assessed with linear regression models adjusted for baseline values, treatment, and the aforementioned stratification factors. The same analysis was performed to assess the treatment effect compared with baseline during titration. No imputation was performed. The numbers of nonmissing observations by visit and treatment group are available in Table S2. Given the differential completion of visits after 36 weeks (time of primary end point), the treatment effect was also assessed at weeks 48 and 60 with the available data at each visit without imputation as a sensitivity analysis.
The treatment effect on mitral regurgitation was assessed with ordinal logistic regression adjusted for baseline mitral regurgitation and the stratification factors.

Additional sensitivity analyses for the treatment effect among those without atrial fibrillation (those without atrial fibrillation on baseline ECG [prespecified definition that is distinct from the stratification factor for atrial fibrillation] and those without history of paroxysmal atrial fibrillation or flutter) were performed with linear regressions adjusted for baseline values, treatment, and presence of intracavity obstruction. For echocardiographic parameters with substantial baseline variability, sensitivity analyses were performed with log-transformed outcomes. Baseline-adjusted linear regression models identical to the primary analyses were fit with log-transformed week 36 and baseline values, and exponentiated treatment coefficients were reported as adjusted geometric mean ratios with 95% CIs. Assessment for treatment interaction with the presence of investigator reported intracavity obstruction was also performed.

Linear regression models were used to evaluate the association between changes in pVO2 and KCCQ-CSS and changes in echocardiographic measures after adjustment for respective baseline values and stratification factors with results presented as stratified by treatment. The model was fitted within each treatment group separately. NT-proBNP was log-transformed before inclusion in regression models.

For all analyses, values of P<0.05 were considered statistically significant. No adjustments were made for multiple comparisons. All analyses were performed with STATA (version 18.0, StataCorp, College Station, TX).
Data-Sharing Statement

Qualified researchers may submit a request containing the research objectives, end points/outcomes of interest, a statistical analysis plan, data requirements, a publication plan, and qualifications of the researcher(s). Requests are reviewed by a committee of internal and external advisors. If approved, information necessary to address the research question will be provided under the terms of a data-sharing agreement. Data-sharing requests will be considered after applications for marketing authorization in the United States and Europe have been reviewed and final decisions rendered. There is no end date for eligibility to submit a data-sharing request for this study. Requests may be submitted to medicalaffairs@cytokinetics.com.
Results

Of the 517 ACACIA-HCM participants, 258 were randomized to aficamten and 259 to placebo. Mean±SD age was 55±16 years (54% female, 75% White, 13% Asian). Baseline characteristics were similar between groups (Table S3). Investigators reported 42 participants with evidence of persistent atrial fibrillation and 47 participants with evidence of intracavity obstruction; these groups made up the stratification factors for analysis.
Baseline Echocardiographic Findings

At baseline, the mean±SD LVEF was 68±4%, mean maximum wall thickness was 2.3±0.5 cm, indexed LV end-diastolic volume was low (35.0±7.1 mL/m2), and LAVI was mildly increased (38.3±14.1 mL/m2). Mean LV global longitudinal strain was impaired and diastolic function was abnormal, with reduced septal e’ velocity (5.1±1.7 cm/s) and elevated septal E/e’ (15.4±7.1), low normal lateral e’ velocity (7.6±2.6 cm/s), and borderline lateral E/e’(10.5±5.2). Mean LV global circumferential strain was normal to hyperdynamic, consistent with the hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) population. Mean peak tricuspid regurgitant velocity was at the upper limit of normal (257.1±38.7 cm/s), and measures of RV size and function (RV fractional area change, 39.0±4.8%; RV s’ velocity,12.3±2.6 cm/s; tricuspid annular plane systolic excursion, 2.2±0.4 cm) were within the normal range (Table 1). At baseline, mitral regurgitation was present in 172 of 449 participants (mild, 142 [32%]; moderate, 24 [5%]; and severe, 6 [1%]) after the exclusion of those with missing data at baseline, week 36, and EoT (68 [13%]; aficamten, 39; placebo, 29).
Baseline and Change in Echocardiographic Measures Over 36 Weeks and EoT
Treatment Effect of Aficamten on Echocardiographic Measures

The treatment effect was evaluated at week 36 and at EoT (median time to EoT, 49 weeks [interquartile range, 43, 61]). Compared with placebo, aficamten decreased LVEF (−4.6% [95% CI, −5.5, −3.6]; P<0.001), decreased LV global circumferential strain (1.2% [0.8, 1.7]; P<0.001), increased LV volumes (LV end-diastolic volume index, 4.1 mL/m2 [2.8, 5.4]; LV end-systolic volume index, 3.2 mL/m2 [2.5, 4.0]; P<0.001 for all), increased LV linear dimensions (LV end-diastolic diameter, 0.1 cm [0.03, 0.2]; P=0.007; LV end-systolic diameter, 0.3 [0.2, 0.4]; P<0.001), and decreased maximum wall thickness −0.1 cm [−0.2, −0.1]; P<0.001) at 36 weeks (Figures S1 and S2). Modest treatment effects were seen in interventricular septal wall thickness. At 36 weeks, stroke volume (by Doppler) and cardiac output decreased (−10.2 mL [−13.2, −7.3]; −0.6 L/min ([−0.8, −0.3]; P<0.001 for all, respectively), whereas resting heart rate increased mildly compared with placebo (2.2 bpm [0.6, 3.7]; P=0.006). These treatment differences persisted through EoT (Table 1 and Figure 1). Aficamten did not significantly change LV global longitudinal strain.

Aficamten improved lateral e’ and septal e’ velocities at 36 weeks (0.9 cm/s [0.5, 1.2]; 0.7 cm/s [0.4, 0.9], respectively; P<0.001 for both) with a sustained effect throughout the EoT (0.9 cm/s [0.5, 1.2]; 0.9 cm/s [0.6, 1.1], respectively; P<0.001 for all; Table 1, Figure 1, and Figure S1). There was no significant improvement in lateral E/e’ or septal E/e’ at 36 weeks, but significant improvement was detected by the EoT for septal E/e’ (−1.4 [−2.1, −0.6]; P<0.001; Table 1 and Figure 1). Peak E velocity increased at 36 weeks (5.1 m/s [2.2, 8.0]; P=0.001) with a more marginal treatment effect at EoT (2.9 [0.2, 5.5]; P=0.034). LAVI did not significantly improve at 36 weeks (−1.3 mL/m2 [95% CI, −2.6, 0.04]; P=0.058) but showed a trend toward improvement with longer exposure at EoT (−1.7 mL/m2 [−3.2, −0.3]; P=0.022; Table 1 and Figure 2); LAVI appeared to remain stable in the aficamten group compared with a mild increase in size in the placebo group. Peak tricuspid regurgitation velocity decreased significantly more with aficamten both at 36 weeks (−10.4 cm/s [−19.9, −1.0]; P=0.03) and EoT (−13.5 cm/s [−22.2, −4.9]; P=0.002) among those with available data (n=234 at baseline, n=221 at EoT; Table 1). Similar to LV size, RV size increased mildly at 36 weeks (RV end-diastolic area, 1.0 cm2 [0.5, 1.5]; RV end-systolic area, 0.7 cm2 [0.4, 1.1]; P<0.001 for all), which was sustained through EoT (0.6 cm2 [0.1, 1.1]; P=0.020; 0.5 cm2 [0.2, 0.9]; P=0.002, respectively) with reductions in several measures of RV systolic function over 36 weeks and at EoT (RV s’ velocity, −1.1 cm/s [−1.5, −0.8]; P<0.001; tricuspid annular plane systolic excursion, −0.1 cm [−0.2, −0.03]; P=0.005; Table 1).

Among those with available data, mitral regurgitation severity did not significantly change at week 36 (aficamten: mild, 77 [35%]; moderate, 22 [10%]; and severe, 0 [0%]; placebo: mild, 75 [33%]; moderate, 11 [5%]; severe, 2 [1%]; odds ratio, 1.5 [95% CI, 0.98, 2.2]; P=0.06) or EoT (aficamten: mild, 66 [30%]; moderate, 17 [8%]; and severe, 2 [1%]; placebo: mild, 74 [32%]; moderate, 8 [3%]; severe, 1 [0.4%]; odds ratio, 1.3 [95% CI: 0.9, 2.0]; P=0.18).
Relationship Between Changes in Outcomes and Changes in Echocardiographic Measures

Aficamten significantly improved KCCQ-CSS by a least-squares mean difference of 3 points (95% CI, 0.5, 5.5), pVo2 by 0.67 mL·kg−1·min−1 (0.22, 1.11), and reduced NT-proBNP by 43% (0.38, 0.47) at 36 weeks compared with placebo with a least-squares mean change from baseline of 11.4 points (95% CI, 9.6, 13.2) in KCCQ-CSS score, 0.64 mL·kg−1·min−1 (0.32, 0.95) in pVO2, and 43% (39, 46) reduction in NT-proBNP in the aficamten group. Among those treated with aficamten, improvement in KCCQ-CSS (by 5 units) at 36 weeks was associated with a 0.2-unit decrease in septal E/e’ (Table 2). Changes in clinical outcomes were not associated with changes in measures of RV function among those treated with aficamten; however, an improvement of KCCQ-CSS (5 points) was associated with a decline in RV S’ velocity and an increase in RV fractional area change among the placebo group. An improvement in pVO2 (by 1 unit) at Week 36 was associated with a 0.1 cm/s increase in septal e’. A 50% reduction in NT-proBNP was associated with a 1.1 mL/m2 decrease in LAVI, 0.3 cm/s increase in lateral e’ velocity, 0.4 cm/s increase in septal e’ velocity, and 1.0 decrease in septal E/e’. Improvement in KCCQ-CSS and NT-proBNP was significantly associated with small reductions in maximal wall thickness measurements (Table 2).
Relationship Between Change in Outcomes and Change in Select Echocardiographic Measures
Titration and Washout

Incrementally larger improvements in measures of LV structure and diastolic function compared with placebo were observed as doses were increased at weeks 2, 4 and, 6 (Figures 1 and 3 and Table 3). After the 4-week washout period, the treatment effect was attenuated with echocardiographic measures returning to near baseline (Table 3).

Sensitivity Analyses

Because there is differential completion of visits after week 36, the treatment effects of echocardiographic measures at weeks 48 and 60 were also assessed with the observations available. Table S4 demonstrates similar effect sizes over time despite fewer participants with some variability in P value significance, likely in part limited by the smaller sample sizes (numbers of observations by visit and treatment group are available in Table S2). Although those with atrial fibrillation on baseline ECG were excluded from the assessment of the treatment effect on LAVI, no significant difference in treatment effect was observed in other measures of diastolic function among participants with and without atrial fibrillation on baseline ECG or history of paroxysmal atrial fibrillation or flutter (Table S5). Sensitivity analyses using log-transformed echocardiographic measures yielded findings consistent with the primary analysis (Table S6). No significant interaction with treatment was present with those with investigator-reported intracavity obstruction; however, this group included only 47 participants. LVEF assessment was similar between core laboratory–reported (−4.6% [−5.5, −3.6]; P<0.001) and site-reported (−4.0% [−5.0, −2.9]; P<0.001) measurements with no significant treatment-by-site interaction (P=0.29; Figure S3).
Discussion

Among the symptomatic nHCM participants in ACACIA-HCM, aficamten improved several measures of cardiac structure and function. Specifically, several measures of LV diastolic function improved and some structural measures were preserved compared with placebo. Although much of the clinical benefit of aficamten in oHCM has been attributed to relief of LV outflow tract obstruction, these findings provide new insights into the cardiovascular effects of aficamten in patients with symptomatic nHCM.

Abnormal diastolic function is present in most patients with HCM with and without obstruction and can be present in the absence of symptoms. Impaired diastolic function appears to be an early, fundamental manifestation of HCM that may precede the emergence of clinically overt disease and symptoms. Among 4 measures of abnormal diastolic function (septal e’ <7 cm/s, septal E/e’ >15, LAVI >34 mL/m2, and peak tricuspid regurgitation velocity >280 cm/s) in a study of 290 patients with HCM, the presence of at least 3 abnormal values was associated with a higher incidence of HCM-related adverse outcomes over a median follow-up of 9.7 years (interquartile range, 6.9–12.9 years). In the ACACIA-HCM cohort, diastolic function was abnormal at baseline with reduced e’ velocities, elevated and abnormal septal E/e’, mildly dilated LAVI, and high normal peak tricuspid regurgitation velocity, consistent with a higher baseline risk of HCM-related morbidity.

As a next-in-class cardiac myosin inhibitor, aficamten targets the excessive actin-myosin cross-bridges in HCM to reduce contractility, promote cross-bridge detachment, and decrease myocardial energy consumption, processes that are also thought to improve impaired relaxation. Multiple indices of LV diastolic function improved with aficamten in this nHCM population. Both septal and lateral e’ velocity improved at 36 weeks with sustained improvement at the EoT. Septal E/e’ demonstrated significant improvement at the EoT with longer treatment exposure and started with more abnormal baseline values compared with lateral E/e’. The early increase in both e’ and E velocity during titration suggests improvement in myocardial relaxation and enhanced early diastolic filling (transmitral flow). This parallel increase in e’ and E velocities likely contributed to the limited early change in E/e’ despite early reductions in NT-proBNP. With continued therapy, E velocity subsequently declined, resulting in modest but significant reductions in septal E/e’ (Figure 3). Although between-group differences in LAVI marginally reached statistical significance, longitudinal trajectories differed between treatment groups, with a trend toward stabilization of left atrial size with aficamten, whereas LAVI continued to increase in the placebo group. Last, the peak tricuspid regurgitation velocity, a marker of RV systolic pressure (and indirectly of left atrial pressure in the setting of a primary cardiomyopathy), decreased compared with placebo at both 36 weeks (RV–right atrium gradient, −2.4 mm Hg [95% CI, −4.4, −0.4]; P=0.019) and EoT (−3.0 mm Hg [−4.9, −1.0]; P=0.003) among those patients with available measures. Whether this relatively small effect might mitigate later development of pulmonary hypertension in nHCM remains to be seen in longer-term studies. Furthermore, the extent to which reduced RV systolic function contributes to reduced tricuspid regurgitation velocity is unclear.

Minimally clinically important differences in diastolic parameters in response to treatment, especially for patients with nHCM, have yet to be established. Measures of diastolic function tend to progress over time and are associated with adverse cardiovascular outcomes. Data from large, well-characterized, older adult cohorts show progressive worsening of diastolic indices, including LAVI (2.3±6.4 mL/m2), septal e’ (−0.6±1.4 cm/s), and septal E/e’ (3.1±4.4), over a mean of 6.6±0.8 years among those with a mean age of 74±4 years. Among a large, multidecade cohort of Medicare beneficiaries (n=4572) with serial outpatient echocardiograms, the average rate of tricuspid regurgitation velocity progression was 0.23 m/s per year (95% CI, 0.22, 0.23) among those with progression, whereas those with regression (8.4%) over the study period had a substantially lower mortality risk compared with those with progression (adjusted hazard ratio, 0.40 [95% CI, 0.28, 0.57]; P<0.001). Although the improvement in diastolic function in ACACIA-HCM was relatively modest, the diastolic indices notably either stabilized without progressive worsening (LAVI) or suggested continued improvement between 36 weeks and EoT (septal e’, septal E/e’). Similar patterns of stabilization or attenuation of disease progression in cardiac imaging measures have been associated with favorable clinical outcomes in other cardiomyopathies, although whether this applies to nHCM remains to be determined. Longer-term aficamten data will be available in the open-label extension study FOREST-HCM (Follow-Up, Open-Label, Research Evaluation of Sustained Treatment With Aficamten in Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy; NCT04848506) to better evaluate longer-term effects of aficamten on LV diastolic function. It is important to note that aficamten appeared to demonstrate incremental changes during the study titration period with dose escalation with progressive improvement of LV diastolic function measures, including both e’ and E/e’, followed by attenuation of the treatment effect after a 4-week washout, supporting a reversible treatment-related effect on measures of diastolic function.

The association between improvement in diastolic function and the observed clinical and symptom improvement in pVO2, KCCQ-CSS, and NT-proBNP provides further support for the importance of diastolic function in contributing to clinical status and symptoms. The greater magnitude and earlier reduction in NT-proBNP compared with the e’ and E/e’ indices likely reflect the complementary but distinct physiological processes captured by these measures. NT-proBNP is a sensitive marker of myocardial wall stress and responds rapidly to changes in ventricular loading conditions, whereas Doppler indices integrate myocardial relaxation, transmitral flow, and noninvasive estimates of filling pressures that are influenced by loading conditions and other physiological factors. Consequently, changes in biomarkers and echocardiographic measures of diastolic function may evolve differently over time. In addition, producing a marked change in diastolic function parameters with treatment in nHCM may prove more challenging because patients with nHCM more often present with a later stage of disease with more structural abnormalities and fibrosis compared with patients with oHCM, reflecting more established remodeling with variable capacity for reverse remodeling.

In contrast, patients with oHCM demonstrated significant improvement in e’ and E/e’ values by week 24; this higher magnitude of effect and earlier timeline of improvement likely reflect the additional and early effect of aficamten on reducing LV outflow tract gradients, less mitral valve systolic anterior motion, and less mitral regurgitation and its respective contribution to diastolic function. It is important to note that aficamten demonstrates an independent effect on diastolic function in nHCM from that seen in patients with oHCM. Compared with the phase 3 ODYSSEY-HCM trial (A Study of Mavacamten in Non-Obstructive Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy) evaluating mavacamten versus placebo in patients with nHCM and accounting for differences in study design, average E/e’ improved similarly after 48 weeks (serial longitudinal changes and e’ velocities were not reported) with similarly rapid improvements in NT-proBNP, whereas overall LAVI did not significantly change. However, in the ODYSSEY-HCM trial, there was no statistically significant improvement in either KCCQ-CSS or pVO2. Further studies are needed to reconcile these differences and to determine the value of changes in NT-proBNP in the assessment of clinical improvement in nHCM.

Consistent with its mechanism of action, aficamten decreased mean LVEF modestly (−4.6% [95% CI, −5.5, −3.6]) and LV global circumferential strain while remaining within normal range, which is similar to the treatment effect seen with oHCM, with no significant change in LV global longitudinal strain. This reduction in contractility was associated with reversible excursions of LVEF <50% in 27 patients (10.5%) receiving aficamten and 2 receiving placebo (0.8%). Although this occurred at a higher frequency than in the trials with aficamten in oHCM, it represents a substantially lower incidence than that reported in the nHCM cohort enrolled in ODYSSEY-HCM (21.5%), with only 7 patients (2.7%) in ACACIA-HCM requiring a treatment interruption due to low LVEF excursions. If aficamten is approved for use in nHCM, echocardiographic monitoring of LVEF for safety assessment and dose adjustment would be reasonable in clinical management.

Aficamten treatment also resulted in increased LV and RV chamber dimensions, with modest reduction in LV (LVEF) and RV systolic function (RV s’ velocity and tricuspid annular plane systolic excursion). The modest reduction in biventricular systolic function is consistent with the on-target mechanism of action of aficamten and its effect on reducing excessive myosin-actin cross-bridges. These changes are also seen with modest decreases in LV stroke volume (Doppler method) and cardiac output; however, these findings are accompanied by rapid and sustained reductions in NT-proBNP and improvement in KCCQ-CSS and pVO2, which suggests an overall favorable treatment effect. Despite these modest reductions, LV and RV systolic function remained within normal range at the EoT; further study is needed to determine when declines in biventricular function may result in symptomatic LVEF reductions or clinical heart failure and to identify predictors of those who may need more careful monitoring. There was also a modest decrease in maximum wall thickness to a magnitude similar to that seen in other cardiac myosin inhibitor studies. Of note, echocardiographic data from ODYSSEY-HCM were generally similar in regard to increases in LV volumes, reduction in RV function, and reduction in maximum wall thickness. Because there are inherent limitations with wall thickness assessment and LV mass index estimation by echocardiography resulting from assumptions about LV geometry that do not readily translate to the nHCM heart, the cardiac magnetic resonance imaging substudy will provide further evidence for the observed changes in cardiac structure.
Study Limitations

Several limitations should be acknowledged. EoT estimates and treatment effects involved carrying forward the most recent available visit value between weeks 36 and 72; thus, treatment effects at EoT may be attenuated if there is incremental change not otherwise captured between week 36 and EoT. These analyses are exploratory, particularly the estimated treatment effects after week 36 with smaller samples sizes, and no corrections for multiple testing were performed, further underscoring the need for long-term data to support the findings. Echocardiography was performed only at rest, so the diastolic response to exercise and its contribution to improved pVO2 cannot be directly assessed. Without the use of ultrasound enhancing agents, LV volume assessment may be influenced by limited image quality; however, all assessments were performed in a blinded fashion, and any biases would likely be mitigated by randomization. Further evaluation and confirmation of cardiac structure findings will be performed in a cardiac magnetic resonance imaging substudy. Peak tricuspid regurgitation velocity findings are limited by a high degree of missingness due to inherent limitations with tricuspid Doppler image quality; analysis did not use imputed data.
Conclusions

In symptomatic patients with nHCM, aficamten improved multiple measures of LV diastolic function. These findings expand the potential therapeutic effects of cardiac myosin inhibition beyond the reduction of LV outflow tract obstruction observed in prior studies to include favorable effects on diastolic function in nHCM.
